read_from: The route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 1d2470eb356b, store_version 3d8c4ef86c01 (its index.json; the store served on 7 November 2026 AD, 652,885 routes in all), for "Classical Hebrew Words database" (M23): 7,314 routes (axis: routes), 4,089 letters keys (axis: keys). Against the store served on the evening of 6 November 2026 AD, which the ledger of v124.2 counted (7,313 routes of this source), 2 rows stand only now and 1 stood only then (axis: routes, by key and text): the rows that stand only now (keys קש, ר) write the Hebrew word a bracket cites in Hebrew letters and points, where the store of 6 November had the old font's keystrokes or no row at all. The definition field of the same row holds the source's whole gloss, read only to understand a route: it equals the route text on 6,942 routes, and the store's cut flag stands on 3 (axis: routes). The ledger of v124.1 read the store of 31 October (commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4); against it the served store has rejoined four rows it had cut inside a round bracket and struck five rows, so 4 routes now hold a semicolon, every one inside a round bracket (axis: routes). The source audit compares each route with the lane's copy of the source, the file classical-hebrew-words.json in ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/classical-hebrew-words-2026-07-12/ (taken from classical-hebrew-words.org on 12 July 2026 AD, 15,084 records, one record for each headword and homonym number, each with one field gloss): 6,946 routes are a whole gloss on their own key and 367 are one part of a gloss between its semicolons (axis: routes), and no route holds a semicolon. So a route is one item of the source's gloss for one headword and homonym number, and for the routes that exist this dictionary is the ask's case of a store that gives each sense its own route; a comma inside a route may still part different meanings (worm, crimson; wing, bird's tail), and no test can tell when it does, which is why those commas rest in a branch. All routes come from that one field of the source, so no test here guesses a kind of field. The store holds 7,207 of the source's records; 7,828 records have no route here: 5,165 have every part of their gloss standing as the same text on the same letters key under another dictionary, 133 have no Hebrew letters or no gloss, and 2,530 this audit did not trace (axis: records), which is the store's matter. 7,256 records have a route on their key and with the 7,828 without one make 15,084; of those with a route, 58 stand through another record's same-text route and the rest through the store's 7,207 records of this source, 9 of which have no route served now, because the served store struck their rows. The audit is evidence about the source and no part of any test. The source's own key to its signs: none found. The copy holds for each record only the fields id, attested_non_hb, proposed_hb, lemma, keystrokes, unicode, hebrew_number, gloss, part_of_speech, hebrew_bible_count, ben_sira_count, dss_count, inscription_count, semantic_field, semantic_section, source_page and at its head only run_date, source_url, complete_set_url, corpus_records_reported, pages_scanned, rows_fetched, public_domain_posture, with no account of a sign. The source's landing page (fetched by this lane on 22 September 2026 AD; corpus-lane-builds/moses-era-metatoggle-v1/fetch/classical-hebrew-words-org.html) says the data is still being proofread, explains that it gives the keystrokes of the old fonts Hebraica II and New Jerusalem, names the Dictionary of Classical Hebrew (DCH), whose first edition it dates 1993 to 2016, and the Dictionary of Classical Hebrew Revised (DCHR), which it dates 2018 to 2028, and promises a page on the dictionary project as coming soon; it explains no sign of the gloss field, says nothing of what the tags DCH and DCHR do in a gloss, and does not name GRD. So every meaning that says what a sign is for begins "unverified:". Only the shapes of ordinary English spelling (the compound hyphen and the possessive apostrophe, straight and curly) do not.

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one Unicode code point; every character of every route of this dictionary lies in the Basic Multilingual Plane, so a code point and a JavaScript string index are the same thing here. A letter is a character of Unicode's Letter category (JavaScript \p{L}), of any script and any case. A digit is a character of Unicode's Number category (\p{N}). A space is the character U+0020 only, and no test uses whitespace of any other kind. Nothing is trimmed: the text is the whole route text as it stands, which is the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def; the text before and the text after the mark are the parts of it on either side of the mark, without the mark. At the start or the end of the text the character directly before or after the mark is none, and none is no letter and no digit. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it; a stop or comma outside them belongs to the sentence. Exactly means character for character, and every string and every list minds case. Begins with means that the first characters are those of the string, and no word end is needed after them. Contains means a run of those characters anywhere, and no word end is needed.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. Not caught above means that no earlier shape of the same mark took the occurrence. A shape's container field is not part of its test unless the test's words name a container: the checker compares it afterwards.
definitions.pair_sides: For a round or square bracket that has a partner: what the pair holds is the text between the opening and the closing bracket (the template's c.group). The pair's left side is the text before its opening bracket, and the pair's right side is the text after its closing bracket. The opening and the closing bracket of a pair are tried against the same tests, in the same order. A bracket that has no partner holds nothing a test can read: its tests are the shapes never_closed, never_opened and in_unbalanced_text, which stand first for their marks.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source's own file gives every record an id and, where it has more than one homonym, a roman numeral in its field hebrew_number (7,071 of 15,084 records; axis: records), and the route store dropped both; two entries under one letters key stand there as separate texts with nothing to tell them apart (example key אדר: its routes come from the source's records 234 (I), 236 (I), 237 (II), 238 (I), 235 (II), 240 (III)). A few route texts keep a remnant of a number in an editor's words, and that is a note, never identity. keys_with_more_than_one_route_text counts senses and homonyms together.

branches.question: Inside some rows the source writes two or more words side by side, each of which could render the Hebrew alone, like: enemy, foe. Should each be its own reading? A row here is one item of the source's gloss for its word; the source parts its items with a semicolon, and the store has already made a new row at each. So words side by side in one row may mean nearly the same thing, and no test can tell when they do not. The same question covers words parted by a stop, a slash or a question mark (murderer. slayer). Rows whose words lean on each other (be dark, dim) are not in this question and stay one reading under either answer.

options.means: The page prints each part as its own reading: enemy, foe prints enemy, and foe. A bracket, a sign or a lead word on one part stays with that part: bud(s), blossom(s) prints bud(s), and blossom(s); gnawing pain, or perh. sinew prints gnawing pain, and or perh. sinew. The comma, stop, slash or question mark at a cut is not printed: messenger? refuter? etc prints messenger, and refuter? etc.
The page prints the row as one reading, as the source writes it: enemy, foe.

branches.question: In some rows a bracket or a short tag stands at the head or the tail of words side by side, and may speak of all of them, like: (female) dweller, inhabitant. Should each word be its own reading? The source does not say whether the bracket or tag speaks of one word or of all.

options.means: The page prints each word as its own reading, and the bracket or tag stays only with the word it touches, even where it speaks of all: (female) dweller, inhabitant prints (female) dweller, and inhabitant.
The page prints the row as one reading, as the source writes it: (female) dweller, inhabitant.

branches.question: In some rows the source gives two names or spellings of one person, people or place side by side, like: Saul, Shaul. Should each be its own reading?

options.means: The page prints each name as its own reading: Saul, Shaul prints Saul, and Shaul. A tag after the second name stays with it: Enoch, Hanoch (pr.n.) prints Enoch, and Hanoch (pr.n.).
The page prints the row as one reading, as the source writes it: Saul, Shaul.

branches.question: A few rows set the word of one edition of the source's dictionary against the word of another, with a slash between them: tamarisk DCH / [DCHR juniper]. Should each side be its own reading?

options.means: The page prints each side as its own reading, with its tag and its bracket: tamarisk DCH / [DCHR juniper] prints tamarisk DCH, and [DCHR juniper].
The page prints the row as one reading, as the source writes it: tamarisk DCH / [DCHR juniper].

branches.question: Some rows hold no rendering at all, only a remark on the word, like: [word in writing exercise]. Should the page print such a row as a reading? Rows that name the full word (abbrev. of nesef) are not in this question and print as they stand under either answer.

options.means: The page prints the row as it stands today: [word in writing exercise].
The page prints no pill for the row. This needs one step of its own from the page, because a declaration can cut a row and cannot leave one out.

not_done_here: This ledger leaves to the store the semicolons of the source's gloss at which the store has made a new route, which is every semicolon outside a round bracket, and every route that holds no mark, because a shape stands only at a mark (the rows with an edition's tag or a number in the pill); it leaves to the ask's rule 3 the 22 routes whose brackets do not balance (axis: routes), which stay whole, the 16 that hold the sign > among them; it leaves to the page the step that the answer no_pill of B05 asks for, since a declaration can cut a row and has no field that leaves a whole row out; and it strikes nothing, naming in store-questions-v1.jsonl the rows it asks the store about.
